title: Government Subpoena Issue Identification — Memorandum to Partner on Grand Jury Subpoena for Insider Trading Investigation

blind.coverage: Read all 52 criteria and the one-line instructions. Read in full: grand-jury-subpoena, intake-memo-tsao, mehta-tsao-phone-email, grayfield-zheng-email-chain, preservation-notice, clearwater-audit-report. Read partially: ic-memo-veridian (through the approval block, not the appendix of sources); code-of-ethics (Sections VI-X in full, the rest by grep); trading-blotter-extract (metadata, purchase rows and the sales-sheet header, plus greps). Also read the judge prompt (rubric_criterion.txt), which tells judges to apply each criterion "as described" and gives no guidance on equivalents, and the solver system prompt. Legal checks: read United States v. R. Enterprises, 498 U.S. 292 (1991), in CourtListener (the Nixon test does not apply to grand jury subpoenas; the "no reasonable possibility" relevance standard under Rule 17(c)). Read Braswell v. United States, 487 U.S. 99 (1988), including its discussion distinguishing Curcio. Did not read Curcio, Kordel, Nixon, Salman, Stringer or Steinhardt directly. Record inconsistencies that do not affect any criterion: iPhone 13 Pro (intake memo) vs iPhone 14 Pro (Mehta email); 605 vs 599 Lexington Avenue; the IC memo gives average daily volume of 120-150K shares while the emails give 1.8-2.2M; the blotter's fund trade GOF-240305-001 (15,000 sh at $41.90 on March 5) matches Marcus Grayfield's personal trade exactly in size, price and date, although the blotter says personal trades are excluded; the intake memo says the confidential 89% ORR came from "publicly available proxy materials". C-023's "spanning January 2023 to present" is slightly off, because Requests 15-16 reach back to 2022; this is trivial. Checked C-026/C-028 against the record: Code of Ethics Section VIII (BYOD) exists and VIII.A(d) gives the firm consent to access Firm-related data on personal devices, so those criteria are fair. I did not look at any other audit of Harvey LAB.

findings.title: C-025 treats the Nixon trial-subpoena test (relevance, admissibility, specificity) as a standard for challenging a grand jury subpoena
findings.explanation: C-025 passes a memo that 'mentions United States v. Nixon standards (relevance, admissibility, specificity)' as the legal standard for challenging this grand jury subpoena. The Supreme Court rejected exactly that in United States v. R. Enterprises. Nixon's multifactor test governs pre-trial subpoenas and does not apply to grand jury subpoenas. The governing test is Rule 17(c)'s 'unreasonable or oppressive' standard, under which a relevance challenge fails unless there is 'no reasonable possibility' the materials will produce relevant information. The criterion is disjunctive (Rule 17(c) and motion-to-quash references also pass), so it will not fail a correct memo. Its harm is that it rewards a memo that misstates the governing law. Related: C-005 lists 'proportionality' as a basis for narrowing. That is a civil Rule 26 concept with no footing in grand jury practice, but it is one option among several correct ones, so the effect is minor.

evidence.quote: or mentions United States v. Nixon standards (relevance, admissibility, specificity)
SUBPOENA DUCES TECUM (Grand Jury) ... Issued Pursuant to Federal Rule of Criminal Procedure 17(c)
referencing concepts such as relevance, proportionality, undue burden, or Fed. R. Crim. P. 17(c) standards

authorities.citation: United States v. R. Enterprises, Inc., 498 U.S. 292, 298-301 (1991)
authorities.proposition: The Nixon relevancy/admissibility/specificity test for trial subpoenas does not apply to grand jury subpoenas; a relevance-based motion to quash must be denied unless there is no reasonable possibility the materials will produce information relevant to the general subject of the investigation.
Set the relevancy/admissibility/specificity test for pre-trial Rule 17(c) subpoenas (read only as quoted in R. Enterprises).

findings.suggested_fix: Remove the Nixon clause, or reword to: 'references Rule 17(c)'s unreasonable-or-oppressive standard / R. Enterprises (and does not treat Nixon's trial-subpoena test as governing)'. Drop 'proportionality' from C-005 or mark it as a civil analogy.

findings.title: Three criteria depend on explicit risk-severity ratings that the instructions never request
findings.explanation: The instructions ask only for 'a detailed issues memo to the lead partner.' C-044 requires risk-severity ratings or equivalent prioritization. C-045 and C-046 then require the spoliation and conflict issues to be rated 'critical or high (or equivalent top-tier severity).' A competent memo can treat spoliation and the joint-representation conflict as urgent in its text without assigning labeled tiers. That memo falls between C-045/C-046's PASS condition (rated critical/high) and FAIL condition (rated moderate/low). Because the judge prompt tells judges to apply criteria 'as described,' with no equivalence guidance, an unlabeled memo risks failing all three. Prioritizing issues is common in partner memos, which is why this is arguable rather than problematic. Still, a labeled severity scale is a house format, not an implicit part of an issues memo, and three all-pass criteria rest on it.

evidence.quote: Review the attached grand jury subpoena and related client documents and prepare a detailed issues memo to the lead partner.
PASS if the memorandum rates the spoliation/document preservation issue ... as critical or high risk severity ... FAIL if spoliation is rated as moderate or low risk.
PASS: The agent's output satisfies the criterion as described

findings.suggested_fix: Either add 'assign a risk rating to each issue' to the instructions, or reword C-045/C-046 to pass when the memo treats the issue as among the most urgent or requiring immediate action, whether or not it uses labels.

findings.title: C-043 fails the whole memo if any single issue section lacks a recommendation
findings.explanation: C-043 fails the memo 'if any issue section lacks' a description, a subpoena or fact reference, and a recommended course of action. Other criteria require analytic sections that do not naturally end in an action item, for example the exposure assessment in C-035 to C-038 (the March 3/March 4 timing, the March 12 call, the tipper-tippee theory, entity exposure) and the evidentiary assessment of the March 23 email. A competent memo often puts recommendations in a consolidated strategy section, which C-040 itself requires, rather than repeating them in each analytic section. Under a literal judge, one recommendation-free exposure section fails the memo. The instructions specify no per-section template.

evidence.quote: FAIL if any issue section lacks one or more of these three elements.
PASS if the memorandum includes a concluding section that sets out a recommended overall response strategy

findings.suggested_fix: Change to 'the principal subpoena-response issue sections generally include...' or accept recommendations placed in a consolidated strategy section.

findings.title: C-019 requires Braswell or the 'collective entity' label for an oral-testimony issue governed more directly by Curcio/Kordel
findings.explanation: Attachment B demands oral grand jury testimony from a corporate designee. Braswell addresses the custodian's act of producing documents. Braswell itself distinguishes Curcio: a custodian 'cannot lawfully be compelled ... to condemn himself by his own oral testimony.' So the closest authorities for C-018/C-020's designee problem are Curcio and Kordel (the entity must designate someone who can answer without self-incrimination). C-019 fails a memo that correctly relies on Curcio/Kordel and Hale v. Henkel (a corporation has no Fifth Amendment privilege) unless the judge accepts that as the 'collective entity doctrine' without the name. Its phrase 'custodian/designee acts in a representative capacity' also blurs the document/testimony line. C-018's 'tension' language keeps the rubric coherent overall, so this is arguable rather than wrong law.

evidence.quote: FAIL if neither Braswell nor the collective entity doctrine is mentioned in this context.
You are hereby commanded to designate and produce a corporate representative or representatives ... prepared to testify on behalf of the entity before the Grand Jury

authorities.proposition: A custodian may not resist a subpoena for corporate records on Fifth Amendment grounds, but the Court distinguishes Curcio, under which a custodian cannot be compelled to incriminate himself by oral testimony.
A union custodian could not be compelled to give oral testimony about the whereabouts of records (read only as quoted in Braswell).

findings.suggested_fix: Accept Braswell, Curcio, Kordel, Hale v. Henkel/Bellis, or any accurate statement that the entity has no Fifth Amendment privilege while its designee keeps a personal privilege for oral testimony.

findings.title: C-041 requires a 'proposed timeline' for USAO negotiations, which the instructions never request
findings.explanation: C-041 fails a memo without a 'proposed timeline with concrete steps.' An issues memo that recommends calling the AUSA promptly, seeking an extension, negotiating scope and proposing rolling production (which C-004 and C-024 already require) has given the substance. Whether that counts as a 'timeline' is unclear to a literal judge, who may expect dated or sequenced milestones. The requirement partly duplicates C-024 and adds a format demand the instructions do not state.

evidence.quote: FAIL if no proposed timeline with concrete steps is included.
PASS if the memorandum recommends seeking an extension of the return date and/or negotiating a rolling production schedule

findings.suggested_fix: Pass if the memo sets out concrete, sequenced next steps with the USAO; dates not required.

findings.title: C-049 requires noting the subpoena's lack of a privilege-log provision, a narrow checklist item
findings.explanation: The observation is accurate: the subpoena has no privilege-log or clawback instruction, only 'non-privileged' in the certification instruction. Rule 17 has no privilege-log requirement comparable to civil Rule 45(e)(2). A competent memo will deal with privilege handling through the Clearwater and Ridgeline analysis, the fact that the definitions of 'You' and the instructions sweep in documents held by attorneys and consultants, and a recommended non-waiver/clawback agreement, without framing any of this as the 'absence' of a log provision. The FAIL trigger is tied to that specific framing, so a memo that recommends a privilege protocol but does not remark on the missing provision may fail.

evidence.quote: FAIL if the absence of a privilege log provision is not mentioned.

"You" or "Your" means Grayfield Capital Partners, LLC ... and their respective officers, directors, partners, members, managers, employees, agents, representatives, attorneys, accountants, and consultants.

findings.suggested_fix: Pass if the memo recommends a privilege-handling protocol (log, clawback/non-waiver agreement) with the USAO, whether or not it notes the provision is missing.

findings.title: AUSA's name is an apparent anonymization artifact ('Jonathan Cromdale Consulting', email jonathan.mercer@usdoj.gov) and is repeated in the criteria
findings.explanation: The subpoena names the issuing AUSA 'Jonathan Cromdale Consulting' but gives his email as jonathan.mercer@usdoj.gov, which looks like a find-and-replace artifact. C-024 and C-041 use 'AUSA Cromdale Consulting.' A careful solver might call him 'AUSA Mercer' or flag the discrepancy as a defect in the subpoena. The grading impact is minimal because C-024 accepts 'the USAO' and C-041 lists the name only as an example, but the record defect is real and repeated in the rubric text.

evidence.quote: Jonathan Cromdale Consulting Assistant United States Attorney ... Email: jonathan.mercer@usdoj.gov
negotiating a rolling production schedule with AUSA Cromdale Consulting/the USAO

findings.suggested_fix: Make the AUSA's name and email consistent in the subpoena and criteria (and the intake memo).

blind.overall: The rubric mostly tracks the record: the facts behind C-001 to C-016, C-026 to C-039 and C-050 to C-052 are supported by the intake memo, the subpoena, the Clearwater report, the Code of Ethics and the emails, and most legal points (Clearwater privilege, Upjohn, Salman-style personal benefit, the conflict under Rules 1.7/1.13, the spoliation timing) are sound. The one clear legal error is C-025: it credits the Nixon trial-subpoena test as a standard for challenging a grand jury subpoena, which R. Enterprises rejected. Because that criterion is disjunctive, it rewards wrong law rather than failing correct memos. The main all-pass risk is structural: three criteria (C-044 to C-046) depend on severity ratings the instructions never ask for, C-043 requires every issue section to carry a recommendation, and C-041 and C-049 are narrow checklist or format items. C-019's insistence on Braswell or the collective-entity label fits oral designee testimony imperfectly. A strong memo would likely pass most criteria, but a competent memo without labeled severity tiers or with a different structure faces real risk under a judge that applies each criterion 'as described'.

sol_verdicts.reason: I agree. C-025 passes a memo that 'mentions United States v. Nixon standards (relevance, admissibility, specificity)'. R. Enterprises, 498 U.S. at 299-300 (read this session), holds that 'the Nixon standard does not apply in the context of grand jury proceedings.' The criterion is disjunctive, so it will not fail a correct memo. It does reward a memo whose only stated standard is the wrong law.

The criteria ask defense counsel to flag overbreadth and resist investor disclosure. That is the mainstream negotiation posture. The record supports it: the intake memo says Fund III and Credit Partners 'had no involvement in Veridian-related trading whatsoever'. None of these criteria requires claiming that a court would quash. R. Enterprises puts no initial burden on the government, which makes C-032's 'absent a government showing' loose as law. It is still a reasonable position to take with the AUSA, so this is ordinary disagreement about judgment.

C-018 states the tension correctly: the entity has no privilege, but the designee keeps a personal one. It fails nobody who is right. C-019 requires Braswell or the collective-entity label, and it frames the issue as a custodian acting in a representative capacity. Attachment B demands oral testimony, where the closer authorities are Curcio and Kordel. A memo that relies correctly on Curcio, Kordel or Hale may fail C-019.

C-037 fails a memo only if 'the tipper-tippee theory and the Ashford-Grayfield family relationship are not connected'. A careful memo that treats the relationship as supporting a Salman gift-to-relative benefit, with the tip itself still to be proven, passes. Within a tipping theory, the phrase 'family relationship ... providing the personal benefit' is standard shorthand, and nothing requires the memo to overstate it. The record supports the brother-in-law relationship, Ashford's SAB access and the March 12 call.

C-023 fails only if the return-date issue is 'not flagged'. The facts check out: June 5 to July 8 is 33 days, with 18 requests and 11 topics, and the intake memo itself asks how to get an extension. C-040, C-047 and C-048 describe things any detailed subpoena memo will contain. The real risks are the labeled severity tiers in C-044 to C-046, which the instructions never request, and C-043's rule that every section must have all three elements.

findings.title: C-025 credits Nixon's trial-subpoena test (relevance, admissibility, specificity) as a standard for challenging a grand jury subpoena
findings.explanation: C-025 passes a memo that 'mentions United States v. Nixon standards (relevance, admissibility, specificity)' as the legal standard for challenging this grand jury subpoena. R. Enterprises holds that the Nixon standard does not apply to grand jury proceedings. A Rule 17(c) relevance challenge must be denied unless there is 'no reasonable possibility' the materials will produce relevant information, and the government bears no initial burden. The criterion is disjunctive, so a correct memo that cites Rule 17(c) or a motion to quash still passes. The defect is that it rewards a memo whose only stated standard is the wrong law, and such a memo would mislead the partner about how hard it is to quash.

evidence.quote: or mentions United States v. Nixon standards (relevance, admissibility, specificity)
Issued Pursuant to Federal Rule of Criminal Procedure 17(c)

authorities.citation: United States v. R. Enterprises, Inc., 498 U.S. 292, 299-301 (1991)
authorities.proposition: 'The Nixon standard does not apply in the context of grand jury proceedings'; a relevance-based motion to quash must be denied unless there is no reasonable possibility the materials will produce information relevant to the general subject of the investigation; placing an initial burden on the Government is error.

findings.suggested_fix: Delete the Nixon clause, or accept Nixon only where the memo distinguishes it. Require Rule 17(c)(2)'s unreasonable-or-oppressive standard as applied in R. Enterprises.

findings.title: C-005 lists civil 'proportionality' as a legal basis for narrowing a grand jury subpoena
findings.explanation: C-005 accepts 'relevance, proportionality, undue burden, or Fed. R. Crim. P. 17(c) standards' as the legal basis for narrowing requests. Proportionality is a civil Rule 26(b)(1) concept with no footing in Rule 17(c) grand jury practice. A memo that invokes only proportionality would pass on a wrong legal basis. The effect is minor because the list is illustrative and most memos will cite Rule 17(c) or burden.

evidence.quote: referencing concepts such as relevance, proportionality, undue burden, or Fed. R. Crim. P. 17(c) standards

authorities.citation: United States v. R. Enterprises, Inc., 498 U.S. 292, 301 (1991)
authorities.proposition: Grand jury subpoena challenges proceed under Rule 17(c)'s reasonableness limits, not trial or civil discovery standards.

findings.suggested_fix: Drop 'proportionality' or label it a negotiation argument by analogy, not a legal standard.

findings.title: C-019 requires Braswell or the 'collective entity' label for oral designee testimony, where Curcio and Kordel are the closer authorities
findings.explanation: Attachment B demands oral grand jury testimony from a corporate designee. Braswell concerns a custodian's act of producing documents, and Braswell itself distinguishes Curcio: a custodian cannot be compelled to incriminate himself by oral testimony. For the designee problem, the closer authorities are Curcio and Kordel, under which the entity must designate someone who can testify without self-incrimination. C-019 may fail a memo that relies correctly on Curcio, Kordel or Hale v. Henkel. Its phrase 'custodian/designee acts in a representative capacity' also blurs the line between documents and testimony. final.changes_from_blind: I split blind O1. C-025 stays problematic (O1). The C-005 proportionality point is now a separate arguable finding (O2), so each finding carries one status. This session I re-verified R. Enterprises in CourtListener, including the passage 'the Nixon standard does not apply in the context of grand jury proceedings' and the no-initial-burden holding. I marked Braswell and Curcio unverified because I did not reread them this session. I did not adopt Sol F2 (C-001 to C-003, C-031, C-032) or Sol F4 (C-037): the positions in those criteria are reasonable, and their FAIL conditions do not fail correct work. From Sol F5, I added nothing beyond blind O2 and O3. I reviewed C-023, C-040, C-047 and C-048 and found no defects. All other blind findings (O2 to O7) are retained and renumbered O3 to O8.
final.overall: The rubric tracks the record well, and most of its legal points are sound. The one clear legal error is C-025. It credits the Nixon trial-subpoena test for a grand jury subpoena, which R. Enterprises expressly rejects. Because C-025 is disjunctive, it rewards wrong law rather than failing correct memos. The main all-pass risk is structural. C-044 to C-046 depend on severity tiers the instructions never request, C-043 requires every issue section to carry all three elements, and C-041, C-049 and C-019 are narrower than the legal substance they target. I reject Sol's overbreadth, investor (F2) and Salman (F4) concerns: those criteria take reasonable defense-counsel positions and would not fail competent work.
final.coverage: In the blind pass I read all 52 criteria and the instructions, and read the key documents in full (subpoena, intake memo, emails, preservation notice, Clearwater report). In this pass I re-checked the criteria Sol raised (C-001 to C-003, C-018, C-019, C-023, C-025, C-031, C-032, C-037, C-040, C-043 to C-048) plus C-005, C-020, C-024, C-035, C-038, C-041 and C-049 against the subpoena and intake memo text. I verified that R. Enterprises holds Nixon inapplicable, sets the no-reasonable-possibility standard and places no initial burden on the government (CourtListener opinion 112523). I read Sol's audit markdown and index entry. I did not re-read Braswell, Curcio or Salman this session.
